title: How to Waste a Teacher
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Responding to Khan Academy's Chief Academic Officer Kristen DiCerbo, Dan Meyer argues that the real threat edtech poses to teaching isn't replacement -- almost no teacher he's spoken with fears being replaced by AI -- but waste: most edtech products have no real model of what teachers do and consequently fail to make use of what experienced teachers bring to the classroom. His diagnostic test is simple: if the ways teachers interact with a piece of software improve as the teacher gains more experience, pedagogical knowledge, technological fluency, or socioemotional skill, the tool has formed a genuine partnership with teachers; if those interactions stay flat regardless of experience, the tool is wasting them. He contrasts this with his own work at Desmos and Amplify, where experienced teachers had real influence over product direction, giving teachers meaningful roles that use their skill rather than reducing them to login-facilitators. Meyer closes with an 'Odds & Ends' section contrasting Sal Khan's 2023 optimism about AI's transformative potential with DiCerbo's more recent, more cautious framing, plus a swipe at Margaret Renkl's New York Times argument that letting AI structure your writing flattens human thought.
points: Meyer's core diagnostic for whether an edtech tool respects teachers: does usefulness scale with a teacher's years of experience, pedagogical knowledge, and socioemotional skill, or is a 15-year veteran's interaction with the software identical to a first-year novice's?

He explicitly separates two different critiques of edtech -- 'trying to replace teachers' (which he says almost no working teacher actually worries about) from 'wasting teachers' (his actual claim) -- to sharpen where the real problem lies.

The Desmos/Amplify counterexample shows what a non-wasteful partnership looks like: opinionated, experienced teachers given real influence over product design rather than treated as an implementation layer.

The Sal Khan (2023) vs. Kristen DiCerbo (2025) quote pairing tracks how even AI-optimist rhetoric inside edtech has cooled from 'the biggest positive transformation education has ever seen' to 'cautiously optimistic... not the Golden Ticket.'
quotes: My point, instead, is that Khan Academy, like most edtech, wastes teachers. This isn’t so much a worry or a critique as it is a statement of fact: much of edtech has no idea what teachers do and consequently wastes them.

If those interactions improve when a teacher has more years of experience, more pedagogical content knowledge, more technological fluency, more socioemotional skill, etc, then you have formed an effective partnership with teachers. If they don’t, then you haven’t.

The best that a lot of edtech can hope for is an additive relationship with teachers across the experience continuum. A 15-year veteran teacher can log kids into a website just as well as a first-year novice. The veteran’s skills are wasted by the tool.
At Desmos and Amplify, a bunch of very opinionated and very experienced teachers had an uncommon level of influence over edtech product direction.
DiCerbo, meanwhile, says “the teacher is fundamental to this whole process,” but she doesn’t say how and that is where her answer ends.
